paper_title: RAP: A Dataset for Paper-to-Poster Generation via Declarative Markup from Human-Crafted Exemplars

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Making a conference poster is visual coding in miniature: an entire paper must be compressed onto a single page, which exercises summarization, visual design, and code implementation at once, using nothing beyond the paper itself. Yet benchmarks for this task in the context of visual coding remain scarce: existing resources are small and annotated only with layout boxes, so evaluation must fall back on VLM-as-judge or human checklists rather than objective render-and-compare, and the generation methods they support design layouts from scratch, leaving human-crafted posters unusable as either a retrievable design library or as verified supervision. We introduce RAP (Reconstruct A Poster), a dataset and benchmark for paper-to-poster generation as a visual coding task. RAP contains 25K+ verified paper-poster pairs from various machine learning conferences held between 2022 and 2026, annotated with a three-level content taxonomy, plus a held-out benchmark of 150 test papers each paired with its human poster. A fully automated derendering pipeline turns each poster into styled HTML/CSS of typed, refillable slots, so every sample is a paper-poster-markup triplet verifiable by rendering against the source poster. The corpus serves both inference and training: PosterRAG, a training-free multi-agent pipeline, retrieves an exemplar and refills its slots without touching layout or styling, while an SFT+RL recipe trains a dedicated model from the same triplets. An online demo is available at https://reconstruct-a-poster.github.io/.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Automatically condensing scientific paper into conference poster is an ideal yet long-overlooked validation task for visual coding. The task exercises three capabilities that are individually measurablesummarization, layout and visual design, and code implementation: model must extract the salient content of full-length paper, organize that content into clear layout with coherent visual design under limited space and fixed aspect ratio, and render the result legibly for human readers. All three draw solely on information that the paper itself supplies, so every model operates on identical inputs, free from the variance introduced by web search. However, existing benchmarks remain limited in scale, annotation depth, and utilization. First, scale and verifiability. Paper2Poster provides 100 paper-poster pairs [1] and P2PEval 121 [2]. Larger collections supply abstracts [3] or full papers for only 100 of 7,855 posters [4]. SciPostGen pairs 18,097 papers and posters but targets layout-level annotation [5]. Generation benchmarks rely on subjective, costly VLM judgments or human checklists [1, 2] rather than direct render-and-compare verification, limiting reproducibility and statistical robustness. Second, task formulation and annotation depth. Resources annotate boxes, categories, reading order, and hierarchy [4, 6], but lack renderable markup reconstructing source posters for end-to-end visual coding. Third, utilization. Methods largely generate layouts from scratch, while template-based system retrieves from few curated slides [7]. P2PInstruct supplies model-generated rather than human-grounded HTML designs [2]. Existing resources lack reusable human-crafted design libraries and verified paper-poster supervision for generator training. Table 1 summarizes these gaps. Table 1: Comparison of representative scientific poster datasets and benchmarks. Our resource links full papers and human-crafted poster exemplars to reconstructed, styled HTML with typed, refillable content slots. *P2PInstruct counts instructionresponse pairs with synthetic instruction/HTML targets; human-crafted posters serve as generation references. Full-paper coverage is partial: 100 posters in SciPostLayout; SciPostLayoutTree inherits partial coverage through SciPostLayout.

sections.title: Annotations
sections.content: SciPostLayout [4] PosterSum [3] Paper2Poster [1] P2PEval [2] SciPostLayoutTree [6] SciPostGen [5] P2PInstruct [2] 7,855 16,305 100 121 7,849 18,097 30,460 RAP (Ours) 25,435 * Boxes Abstracts, topic labels QA pairs Checklists Boxes, OCR, reading order, hierarchy Boxes, OCR, figure/table links Instructions, figure descriptions, text, HTML Boxes, OCR, HTML, figure assets, asset links, design captions, taxonomy We therefore introduce RAP (Reconstruct Poster), dataset and benchmark for paper-to-poster generation as visual coding task. At its core is the largest paper-poster collection to date: 25,435 verified pairs collected from NeurIPS, ICML, and ICLR (20222026) via OpenReview, each enriched with paper-level metadata, distilled introduction summary, and annotations from three-level taxonomy of 15 domains, 20 tasks, and 39 methods that support contentaware retrieval and analysis. Complementing the corpus, we curate held-out benchmark of 150 test papers, 10 per domain, each paired with its ground-truth human poster. Because every sample carries its own human-crafted reference, render-and-compare verification is available at the scale of the whole corpus rather than only on handful of curated examples, making measurement objective and reproducible instead of dependent on judge-based scoring. To demonstrate the datasets utility at both inference time and training time, we develop two applications that exploit its complementary supervision signals. (1) Training-free retrieval-augmented generation. We present PosterRAG, multi-agent pipeline that treats the dataset as reusable design library. hierarchical retrieval cascadecategorical filtering, narrative matching, and aesthetic scoringselects the best-matching exemplar for an input paper; mapping agent then programmatically refills the retrieved templates typed slots with paper content while leaving all layout and styling untouched; and VLM reviewer iteratively repairs residual visual defects. Because PosterRAG inherits humancrafted designs unmodified rather than hallucinating layouts, it achieves state-of-the-art diversity and distributional human-likeness against strong baselines. (2) Post-training dedicated paper-to-poster model. The triplets likewise provide direct inputoutput supervision: we apply supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to multimodal model on papermarkup pairs, then further optimize it with reinforcement learning using verifiable rewards [8]. 2 RAP: Dataset for Paper-to-Poster Generation via Declarative Markup from Human-Crafted Exemplars PREPRINT Our contributions are as follows: large-scale dataset and benchmark. RAP is the largest paper-poster resource to date, comprising 25,435 verified pairs with three-level content annotations and held-out benchmark of 150 test papers. Because every sample carries human-crafted reference, evaluation proceeds by objective render-and-compare rather than by judge-based scoring alone. An automated derendering pipeline. fully automated pipeline converts raster posters into styled, renderable HTML/CSS in which every element is an addressable, typed, and refillable slot. Two dataset-driven applications. PosterRAG, training-free retrieval-augmented pipeline, and an SFT+RL recipe for training dedicated paper-to-poster model demonstrate that the same corpus serves as reusable design library at inference time and as verified supervision at training time.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Visual Coding Data and Benchmarks. Visual coding has emerged as rigorous testbed for multimodal models. pix2code [9] pioneers code generation from GUI screenshots; Design2Code [10] and Vision2Web [11] extend the task to real webpages and multi-page websites, the latter incorporating agent-based verification; Plot2Code [12] and ChartMimic [13] target scientific plots and charts. These benchmarks, however, all overlook the paper-to-poster task: their inputs are screenshots or short specifications of single, self-contained view, whereas poster generation requires condensing full-length paper into space-constrained, information-dense design and implementing it as code. RAP is constructed around the requirements of visual coding: the full paper supplies the long-context input, every poster is derendered into styled, renderable HTML/CSS with typed, refillable slots, and reconstruction fidelity is measured by direct render-and-compare against the human reference, making paper-to-poster, for the first time, visual coding benchmark whose outputs are verifiable at scale. Paper-to-Poster Generation. Existing resources for this task supply posters and, at best, layout-level annotations. Paper2Poster [1] and P2PEval [2] pair papers with only few hundred raw poster images and rely on VLM judges for evaluation; PosterSum [3] pairs posters with abstracts rather than full papers; SciPostLayout and SciPostLayoutTree [4, 6] annotate layout boxes, reading order, and figure correspondence, and SciPostGen [5] does so at larger scale, but none provides renderable markup that reconstructs the poster. Approaches to generation fall into two families. Text-to-image generation. Recent progress in visual text rendering [1416] and in frontier image generators [1721] enables the synthesis of poster-like images directly from prompts. Their outputs, however, are non-editable raster images whose text fidelity degrades sharply on dense scientific content, and they offer no guarantee that the rendered content faithfully reflects the source paper. LLM-based pipelines. Paper2Poster [1], P2P [2], and PosterGen [22] decompose the task into paper parsing, content planning, and markup rendering in HTML or PPTX, typically with multi-agent checking and refinement, whereas PosterLLaVa [23] and PosterLlama [24] fine-tune multimodal models for the content-aware layout sub-problem in isolation. Instruction-tuning data for the task is model-generated rather than human-grounded: P2PInstruct [2] supplies HTML targets synthesized by models rather than derived from human-crafted posters. Document-to-slide systems [7, 25] follow the same parseplanrender paradigm; in particular, PPTAgent [7] retrieves from small set of manually curated slide templates, but its rigid filling mechanism often fails to adapt content appropriately. Both families thus confront common trade-off: either sacrifice editability and content fidelity, or generate layouts from scratch without grounding in human design. RAP addresses both sides of this trade-off: its derendered, human-crafted posters ground retrieval-augmented pipeline that inherits professional designs rather than inventing them, and its paper-poster-markup triplets provide direct supervision for post-training dedicated generation model with reference-based rewards.

sections.title: 3 RAP: Large-Scale Poster Derendering
sections.content:
Data Collection and Statistics. The RAP dataset is built from accepted papers at three top-tier ML conferences from 2022 through 2026. Using OpenReview, we collect raw poster files together with their associated paper records. For each submission, we retrieve three types of information: (i) the paper PDF or LaTeX source when available from supplementary material; (ii) the author-uploaded poster file in either PDF or image format; and (iii) metadata including title, authors, abstract, venue, year, and keywords. We then normalize poster formats and match each poster to its source paper, yielding final dataset of 25,435 verified paperposter pairs distributed across NeurIPS (11,256), ICLR (8,504), and ICML (5,675). Each paper is further enriched with structured annotations, including taxonomy of 15 domains, 20 tasks, and 39 methods, plus distilled introduction summary for narrative-level retrieval (B.1.1). Derendering Pipeline. Our derendering pipeline converts raw poster image into structured HTML template with typed, fillable slots through four stages (Figure 2): Stage 1: Layout Detection. fine-tuned LayoutLMv3 [26] 3 RAP: Dataset for Paper-to-Poster Generation via Declarative Markup from Human-Crafted Exemplars PREPRINT Figure 2: Derendering pipeline illustration. model localizes all visual elements (Title, Plain Text, Figure, Table, Formula, Caption, etc.) with bounding boxes and confidence scores. Each detected element is subsequently assigned to one of three semantic categories: text-like (titles, plain texts, captions), image-like (figures, tables, formulae) or decorative (icons, logos). Stage 2: Font Size Estimation. For each text-like bounding box, the corresponding image region is cropped and processed by PaddleOCR [27]. Text lines are identified by grouping OCR detection results via y-axis overlap, and the font size in pixels is estimated as font_size = (hbbox/nlines) 0.8, where the factor 0.8 accounts for inter-line spacing, yielding conservative estimate directly usable as CSS font-size. Stage 3: Design Captioning. The original poster image alone is passed to an MLLM, which produces structured design caption encoding both global attributes (the page-level color palette, typography family, and decorative motifs) and per-region design dimensions: spatial composition, visual anchor, reading flow, layer interaction, content density, color-scheme roles, typographic hierarchy, emphasis strategy, and border/decoration treatment. Stage 4: HTML Reconstruction. An HTML scaffold is first programmatically constructed with absolute-positioned
elements for each detected block: image-like and decorative regions are cropped from the original image and embedded as elements, while text-like blocks are rendered as empty content slots with their OCR-measured font sizes pre-annotated as styling constraints. The scaffold encodes pixel-exact block geometry but leaves all visual styling (colors, backgrounds, typography, and decorative CSS) as empty placeholders to be filled. The scaffold, the original poster image, and the design caption are then jointly provided to an MLLM, which populates each text-like slot by reading content directly from the poster, applies the pre-annotated font sizes and per-region descriptors, and synthesizes CSS decorations to reproduce the posters visual appearance. The derendering outcome is complete HTML file in which each content block is fully styled, addressable slot that faithfully reproduces the original posters layout and visual appearance.

sections.title: 4 Method
sections.content: Building on our RAP dataset, we develop two applications for high-quality poster generation: PosterRAG: Training-free retrieval-augmented generation, which retrieves and adapts structured templates from our poster bank, and Post-training dedicated paper-to-poster model with our dataset. Figure 3: Two-stage PosterRAG pipeline for multi-agent template retrieval and poster generation. 4 RAP: Dataset for Paper-to-Poster Generation via Declarative Markup from Human-Crafted Exemplars PREPRINT 4.1 PosterRAG: Training-free retrieval-augmented generation As illustrated in Figure 3, PosterRAG consists of two stages: Template Retrieval and Poster Generation. Given an input paper in LaTeX or PDF format, Stage 1 constructs its structured representation Pmeta with ParserAgent and selects the most suitable template from the template bank through three-level RetrievalAgent cascade. Given and Pmeta, Stage 2 produces the final poster ˆT using MappingAgent followed by an iterative ReviewerAgent. ParserAgent. Following Paper2Poster [1], the ParserAgent takes the paper as input and converts it into structured representation Pmeta = {Pd, Pt, Pm, Ps, Pparse}, where Pd, Pt, and Pm denote the domain, task, and method labels of the paper, respectively; Ps the narrative summary, and Pparse the parsed paper content, including text, figures, tables, and formulas. RetrievalAgent-1: Categorical filtering. RetrievalAgent-1 retains templates whose domain, task, and method labels match (Pd, Pt, Pm). Papers with identical labels often share structural patterns, making their templates compatible with the input paper. RetrievalAgent-2: Narrative Matching. RetrievalAgent-2 re-ranks the filtered candidates by comparing the input papers introduction summary Ps with the pre-computed summary of each templates source paper. This comparison captures how papers frame their contributions and emphasize content. For example, paper following gap-and-fill narrative is better matched with template organized around the same problemsolution structure than with one based on an observation-driven narrative. This favors templates whose organization and section emphasis align with the input paper. RetrievalAgent-3: Aesthetic Selection. RetrievalAgent-3 selects the final template by scoring each candidate poster image IT on three independent 15 scales: Content Density, ranging from key-point to full; Visualization Ratio, ranging from text-heavy to figure-heavy; and Scientific Aesthetics, ranging from bare-bones to custom-designed. These scores form sT {1, . . . , 5}3. Without user preferences, the candidate closest to the neutral midpoint is selected; otherwise, VLM converts the preferences into dimension weights to guide the selection. MappingAgent. The MappingAgent fills the typed slots {s1, . . . , sm} of the retrieved template with content from Pmeta in three phases. Slot analysis records each slots ID, type, label, position, and dimensions, estimating text capacity from the slot size and font size and recording the available area for images. Content mapping and adaptation provides an LLM with this slot summary, the importance-ranked paper sections, figures and tables with captions, and pre-rendered assets R. The LLM produces = {(sj, actj, contentj)}, where each action replaces, retains, or clears slot, and the mapped content is adapted to its capacity and section type. Programmatic filling then applies through deterministic dispatcher: text and image slots receive new innerHTML and src values, while unused slots are hidden. During filling, the original layout, typography, colors, and decorative styling remain unchanged, preserving the human-crafted design and full editability. ReviewerAgent. Following Paper2Poster [1], the ReviewerAgent takes the rendered HTML poster ˆT as input and performs iterative visual refinement through see-then-fix process. 4.2 Post-training dedicated paper-to-poster model Figure 4: Post-training pipeline for vision-language model. 5 RAP: Dataset for Paper-to-Poster Generation via Declarative Markup from Human-Crafted Exemplars PREPRINT As illustrated in Fig. 4, we construct training signals from the paper and its reference poster, including paper information and the corresponding user instruction, which serve as input to post-training. The resulting VLM enables users to generate posters tailored to their preferred design and layout. A. Paper Information Extraction. We construct the paper-side input from two complementary components: Paper Text and Paper Assets. The paper text is extracted from method, experiments, and conclusion sections, with sectionspecific budgets used to retain content most relevant to poster generation. For paper assets, we detect tables, images, figures and equations from the PDF, assign unique identifiers, and associate captions based on spatial proximity. We then match the assets to visual slots in the reference poster through visual feature matching and geometric verification, using VLM adjudication for ambiguous cases and leaving uncertain matches unresolved. Assets used in the target poster are retained with their identifiers, metadata, captions, and thumbnails under fixed visual-token budget. The resulting paper-side input is Xpaper = (Tpaper, Apaper) , (1) where Tpaper denotes the section-organized paper text and Apaper denotes the selected assets and their associated information. B. User Instruction Construction. We construct the instruction-side input from two complementary components: Design and Layout. For design, the reference poster is processed by VLM to obtain design description covering its color palette, typography, composition, and visual emphasis. In parallel, attributes such as canvas size and visual density are measured from the ground-truth HTML. The design description and measured attributes are then sampled and verbalized with varying levels of detail and writing styles to form natural-language user request. For layout, the ground-truth HTML is parsed to recover the columns, section order, block geometry, textimage composition, and asset assignments. This structure is converted into layout specification without exposing the exact poster text or HTML implementation. The resulting instruction-side input is Xinstruction = (udesign, slayout) , (2) where udesign is the natural-language user request and slayout is the structured layout specification. Post-training Pipeline. We first perform supervised fine-tuning, followed by rendering-aware reinforcement learning with GRPO. During RL, multiple HTML candidates {Hi}G i=1 are sampled and rendered into poster images Ii = R(Hi), each receiving composite reward: Ri = g(Hi) [λrRrule(Hi) + λvRvlm(Ii, )] , (3) where g(Hi) {0, 1} is validity gate that rejects invalid or non-renderable HTML, is the reference poster, and λr = 0.4 and λv = 0.6 weight the rule-based and model-based rewards, respectively. Rule-based reward rule uses deterministic measurements from the HTML and its rendered Document Object Model (DOM), which provides each elements position, size, and style. It contains three groups. Layout checks text clipping, overlap, out-of-canvas elements, and block correspondence with the reference layout. Density evaluates block and text coverage, empty regions, body font size, and the number of text blocks, preventing sparse outputs produced by deleting content or shrinking text. Assets checks identifier validity, required-figure coverage, broken images, and excess empty image slots. Together, these checks enforce valid layout, sufficient content, and correct asset usage. Model-based reward vlm uses VLM to evaluate the rendered candidate given the reference poster, paper information, and user instruction. It contains two groups. Quality evaluates rendering integrity, legibility, layout, density, content completeness and faithfulness, figure usage, visual design, and instruction adherence. Reference evaluates structural similarity in columns, section order, and block placement, as well as stylistic similarity in colors, typography, and decorations. The weighted dimension scores are reduced by capped penalties for visible defects, providing perceptual assessments of overall quality and reference fidelity.

sections.title: 5 Experiments
sections.content: 5.1 Baselines and Dataset We compare against Nano Banana, P2P [2], Paper2Poster [1], and PosterGen [22]. To ensure fair comparison, all LLM-based agent calls across all methods are replaced with Claude-Opus4.6 [28]. Our evaluation uses held-out test set of papers not included in the 25K template bank. Specifically, we construct the test set of 150 samples by collecting 10 papers from each of the 15 research domains in RAP-25K. 5.2 Evaluation Metrics To evaluate the diversity and human-likeness of generated posters, we assess along two axes. 6 RAP: Dataset for Paper-to-Poster Generation via Declarative Markup from Human-Crafted Exemplars PREPRINT Table 2: Quantitative results for the two dataset-driven poster generation approaches. Best results are in bold, and second-best results are underlined. (a) Template Retrieval-based Generation (b) Post-trained Paper-to-Poster Models Method Diversity Human-likeness Model LPIPS DINOv2-CosDist DISTS FID FDiD Diversity Human-likeness LPIPS DINOv2-CosDist DISTS FID FDiD NanoBanana Pro [18] P2P [2] Paper2Poster [1] PosterGen [22] Ours (Image Guidance) Ours (HTML Guidance) 0.5695 0.5761 0.5547 0.4131 0.5584 0. 0.2364 0.2847 0.1138 0.2710 0.0877 0.4443 0.2231 0.2340 0.2107 0.2527 0.2246 0.3490 24.25 33.24 81.59 133.83 77.11 23. 483.97 377.25 1156.73 682.27 1267.84 306.79 GPT-6-Astra [34] Kimi-K3 [35] Gemini-3.1-Pro [36] Claude-Opus-5 [37] Qwen3.8-27B [38] Qwen3.8-27B-SFT (Ours) Qwen3.8-27B-RL (Ours) 0.5704 0.5856 0.5956 0.6414 0.6284 0.6599 0. 0.2093 0.1974 0.1983 0.2320 0.2579 0.2784 0.2735 0.2369 0.2445 0.2365 0.2728 0.2680 0.2892 0.2944 27.64 27.94 41.49 21.56 32.44 28.00 23. 341.64 340.50 408.05 289.49 465.00 326.24 306.94 Diversity. We measure cross-paper generation diversity by computing pairwise LPIPS [29], DINOv2-CosDist, and DISTS [30] over all pairs of generated posters in the test set, then averaging across pairs. LPIPS captures perceptual diversity via AlexNet features; DINOv2-CosDist measures semantic-level diversity using cosine distances between DINOv2 [31] embeddings; DISTS captures deep structural and textural diversity via VGG features. Higher values indicate more varied generations. Human-likeness. We measure the distributional gap between generated posters and our RAP-25K collection using Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) [32] and Fréchet DINOv2 Distance (FDiD). FDiD replaces InceptionV3 [33] with DINOv2 [31] features, making it sensitive to visual structure and layout geometry. Together, these two metrics quantify the distribution-level fidelity of generated posters to real human-crafted designs. 5.3 Main Results 5.3.1 Quantitative Comparison Table 2(a) shows that RAP (HTML Guidance) achieves the best scores across all five metrics. It attains FID/FDiD of 23.75/306.79, with FDiD 18.7% lower than P2P (377.25), the best baseline on this metric. Its DINOv2-CosDist reaches 0.4443, compared with 0.2847 for P2P and 0.1138 for Paper2Poster. These results support retrieval and adaptation of human-crafted templates for improving both cross-paper diversity and distributional human-likeness. Table 2(b) shows that RAP-based SFT improves all five metrics over the base Qwen3.8-27B. Subsequent RL reduces FID/FDiD from 28.00/326.24 to 23.42/306.94 and increases LPIPS and DISTS, with small decrease in DINOv2CosDist. Among the compared models, our RL variant achieves the highest LPIPS and DISTS and the second-lowest FID/FDiD, behind Claude-Opus-5. These results demonstrate the utility of RAP for improving cross-paper diversity and distributional alignment with human-crafted posters through post-training. 5.3.2 Qualitative Comparison Figure 5 compares posters generated from the same paper. Paper2Poster uses conventional column-based layout, whereas NanoBanana Pro produces more stylized raster poster. RAP (HTML Guidance) follows the retrieved templates color palette, typographic hierarchy, and section organization while adapting its content to the input paper. This example illustrates how human-crafted templates provide reusable design guidance for paper-to-poster generation. Figure 6 compares outputs for the same paper and user instruction. The base Qwen3.8-27B produces largely incomplete poster, whereas both post-trained variants organize text, figures, and tables into complete three-column layouts. Their dark title bands and column organization follow the supplied design specification and resemble the human-crafted reference. This example illustrates improved layout adherence and more complete rendered outputs after post-training. 5.4 Ablation Studies RL reward-component ablations are reported in Appendix B.6. Ablation on HTML Generation. We compare Ours (HTML Guidance), which fills retrieved HTML templates, with Ours (Image Guidance), which generates HTML from poster-image references. HTML Guidance improves all five metrics, reducing FID/FDiD from 77.11/1267.84 to 23.75/306.79. DINOv2-CosDist rises from 0.0877 to 0.4443, alongside higher LPIPS (0.5584 to 0.6471) and DISTS (0.2246 to 0.3490). Unlike image-only guidance, the HTML scaffold explicitly constrains layout and styling while allowing content replacement and refinement. These results support using reconstructed HTML, rather than the reference image alone, to improve distributional human-likeness and cross-paper diversity. 7 RAP: Dataset for Paper-to-Poster Generation via Declarative Markup from Human-Crafted Exemplars PREPRINT Figure 5: Qualitative comparison between PosterRAG (ours) and baseline methods. Figure 6: Qualitative comparison between our post-trained model and other vision-language models. 8 RAP: Dataset for Paper-to-Poster Generation via Declarative Markup from Human-Crafted Exemplars PREPRINT Ablation on derendering. For this poster reconstruction task, we adopt six metrics: SSIM [39] measures pixel-level structural similarity. DISTS [30] measures deep structural and texture dissimilarity. Layout mIoU computes mean IoU between detected and ground-truth layout elements, in both class-aware (mIoU) and class-agnostic (mIoUag) variants. FID [32] and FDiD measure the distributional fidelity to the original poster set. Table 3: Ablation studies on the derendering pipeline. Best results in bold. (b) Pipeline Components (backbone: Claude-Opus-4.6) (a) Backbone Model Pairwise Fidelity SSIM DISTS mIoU mIoUag FID FDiD GPT-4o Qwen-3.5 Gemini-3.1-Pro Claude-Opus-4.6 0.7928 0.7922 0.8076 0.7896 0.1643 0.0966 0.0623 0.0663 0.4692 0.4349 0.6400 0.6897 0.5081 0.4702 0.6706 0.7246 41.00 28.86 17.30 16. 371.41 120.18 66.28 61.71 Base +Layout +Layout +OCR +Layout +OCR +Design (Ours) Pairwise Fidelity SSIM DISTS mIoU mIoUag FID FDiD 0.5843 0.7744 0.7859 0.7896 0.4265 0.0857 0.0686 0.0663 0.0652 0.5236 0.6808 0.6897 0.1069 0.5590 0.7148 0. 53.63 18.32 17.42 16.90 977.20 93.48 65.49 61.71 Backbone model. Table 3(a) compares four backbone MLLMs under the full pipeline. Claude-Opus-4.6 [28] and Gemini3.1-Pro [36] clearly outperform GPT-4o [40] and Qwen-3.5 [41]. Gemini-3.1-Pro achieves the best reconstruction fidelity under SSIM and DISTS, while Claude-Opus-4.6 leads on layout accuracy and distributional fidelity, suggesting it better preserves the structural organization of the original poster. We therefore adopt Claude-Opus-4.6 as the backbone for all other experiments. Pipeline components. Table 3(b) shows that adding Layout yields the largest improvement across all metrics, raising mIoU from 0.0652 to 0.5236. OCR further improves layout accuracy and distributional fidelity, while Design Caption provides smaller but consistent gains across all six metrics. The full pipeline achieves the best reconstruction scores, supporting the complementary roles of geometric, typographic, and design constraints.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: We have cast paper-to-poster generation as visual coding problem and constructed the resource it requires. RAP (Reconstruct Poster) contains 25,435 verified paper-poster pairs from NeurIPS, ICML, and ICLR (20222026), annotated along three-level taxonomy of 15 domains, 20 tasks, and 39 methods, together with held-out benchmark of 150 papers whose human posters are withheld for evaluation. fully automated derendering pipeline rewrites each poster as styled HTML/CSS with typed, refillable slots, reconstructing it faithfully enough (SSIM 0.79, layout mIoU 0.69) that fidelity can be measured by rendering and comparing rather than by judge scoring. These paper-poster-markup triplets support two applications. PosterRAG is training-free: it retrieves human-designed template and refills its slots without disturbing the layout or styling, and it leads every baseline on both diversity and human-likeness. An SFT+RL recipe trains dedicated model against the same references. Together they show that human designs are not merely evaluation yardsticks but reusable source of design knowledge. We release the dataset, derendering pipeline, codebase, and an online demo to make reference-grounded visual coding reproducible setting for future research. AI use statement Claude-Opus-4.6 powered our derendering and RAG pipelines and the agentic baselines; derendering ablations additionally evaluated GPT-4o, Qwen-3.5, and Gemini-3.1-Pro. NanoBanana Pro served as an image-generation baseline. We post-trained Qwen3.8-27B through SFT and RL, using Gemini-3.8-Flash for VLM-based rewards, and compared against its base model, GPT-6-Astra, Kimi-K3, Gemini-3.1-Pro, and Claude-Opus-5. VLMs also assisted training-data construction. AI assistants, including Codex, supported manuscript drafting and language polishing. We retain full responsibility for all research decisions and submitted content. 9 RAP: Dataset for Paper-to-Poster Generation via Declarative Markup from Human-Crafted Exemplars PREPRINT

sections.title: B Implementation Details
sections.content:
B.1 Method B.1.1 POSTERRAG: TRAINING-FREE RETRIEVAL-AUGMENTED GENERATION Stage 1: Template Retrieval. Stage 1 selects the most suitable poster template from the template bank for given input paper. ParserAgent. The ParserAgent converts the raw paper into structured representation Pmeta that drives all downstream retrieval and generation. The parser supports both LaTeX source and PDF input, extracting metadata, segmenting content by section boundaries, and building figure registry of all image assets in PNG format for HTML embedding; the result is parsed content object Pparse = {meta, abstract, sections, figures, tables, formulas}. Beyond content extraction, the ParserAgent classifies the paper into three-level taxonomy by prompting an LLM with the abstract and section titles, producing domain label Pd, task label Pt, and method label Pm. It also distills the introduction into structured summary Ps along four dimensions: motivation, problem formulation, key insight, and claimed contributions, which serves as the semantic fingerprint for narrative-level template matching. Together these form Pmeta = {Pd, Pt, Pm, Ps, Pparse}. RetrievalAgent-1: Categorical filtering. RetrievalAgent-1 performs hard filter, retaining only those templates whose categorical labels exactly match the input papers domain, task, and method. The rationale is that papers sharing the same domain, task, and method tend to follow similar paper structures and argue their contributions in comparable ways, making their posters naturally compatible in layout and content organization. RetrievalAgent-2: Narrative Matching. Beyond category-level structural compatibility, this stage performs finergrained selection by comparing how papers frame their contributions and what content they emphasize. Each templates source paper is associated with pre-computed introduction summary extracted during dataset construction; RetrievalAgent-2 measures the narrative similarity between the input papers Ps and each candidates s, and re-ranks the candidates accordingly. This captures whether two papers share similar narrative logic in their introductions. For instance, paper following gap-and-fill structure (existing methods fail to handle X; we propose to address this) pairs better with template whose source paper argues along the same problemsolution arc, rather than one structured as an observation-driven narrative (experiments reveal that phenomenon occurs under condition Y; motivated by this finding, we derive Z). By matching at the narrative level, RetrievalAgent-2 ensures that the selected templates content layout and section emphasis align with how the input paper tells its story. RetrievalAgent-3: Aesthetic selection. The final retrieval stage selects single template by assessing visual style rather than content. RetrievalAgent-3 scores the poster image IT of each candidate on three mutually independent dimensions on 15 integer scale, producing score vector sT {1, . . . , 5}3: Content Density, from key-point to full, capturing how much of the papers content is reproduced; Visualization Ratio, from text-heavy to figure-heavy, capturing the balance between figures/tables and textual content; and Scientific Aesthetics, from bare-bones to custom-designed, capturing the level of decoration and visual polish. Without user preference, the candidate closest to the neutral midpoint is selected as safe default. When style preferences are provided, VLM-based intent recognizer converts them into per-dimension weights w, shifting selection toward user-emphasized dimensions. Stage 2: Poster Generation. Given the retrieved template and the parsed paper content Pmeta, Stage 2 produces the final poster via MappingAgent that fills the template with paper content, followed by an iterative ReviewerAgent that refines visual quality. MappingAgent. The MappingAgent takes the retrieved template with its typed slots {s1, s2, . . . , sm} and the parsed paper Pmeta, and produces filled poster through three consecutive phases. Slot analysis. The agent profiles each template slot programmatically. For text-like slots, it computes an approximate character capacity derived from their display dimensions (wj, hj) and font size fj; for image-like slots, it records the available dimensions for figure sizing. The result is slot summary describing each slots ID, type, label, spatial position, dimensions, and text capacity. Content mapping and adaptation. An LLM receives the slot summary alongside the papers section content with importance scores, figure and table list with captions, and any prerendered equation or table assets R. It produces mapping = {(sj, actj, contentj)} for every slot, where actj {replace_text, replace_image, replace_rendered, keep, clear} is the fill action, and contentj is adapted from the corresponding source paper element to fit the slots capacity and formatted according to section type (e.g., bullet points for methods, flowing prose for introductions). Programmatic filling. The core insight of our approach is that filling is performed programmatically via direct manipulation rather than LLM-based HTML regeneration. Using deterministic action dispatcher, only slot-level content is updated: text slots receive new innerHTML, image slots receive new src attributes from the figure registry F, and unmapped or stale slots are hidden via visibility flags. 13 RAP: Dataset for Paper-to-Poster Generation via Declarative Markup from Human-Crafted Exemplars PREPRINT All CSS rules, spatial layout, typography, color schemes, gradients, and decorative elements remain exactly as in the original human-created template. This structure-preserving invariant ensures that RAP inherits professional visual design quality while maintaining full editability. ReviewerAgent. Although programmatic filling preserves the templates global structure, inserting new content into fixed slots may still cause visual artifacts such as text overflow, font-size mismatches, poor color contrast, or awkward whitespace. The ReviewerAgent resolves these issues through an iterative see-then-fix loop where each round renders the current HTML poster ˆT into screenshot and uses VLM feedback to guide localized refinements. Visual review. At each round r, headless Chromium browser renders ˆT to pixel-accurate screenshot Ir. The VLM receives Ir along with past fixes, returning an overall score scorer and list of block-level repair suggestions {(bj, issuej, patchj)} specifying the target block ID, issue type, and targeted CSS patch. Constrained refinement. Each patchj is applied locally to its target block bj in ˆT under strict safety constraints that explicitly block destructive modifications across four categories: visibility-hiding rules that would render content invisible to users, text-hostile overflow and truncation properties that cause text to be clipped or hidden, layout geometry alterations that would shift or resize elements, and structural changes to the DOM or color scheme that exceed the intended scope of local refinement. Termination and design rationale. The loop terminates once scorer τscore (default: 8/10), Nmax = 3 rounds are reached, or no further patches are proposed by the agent. Two decisions distinguish this agent from the prior methods [1, 2]: programmatic CSS patching rather than full HTML regeneration ensures layout stability, and screenshot-level feedback detects rendering-dependent defects invisible from source code alone. B.2 Prompt Templates B.2.1 Prompt 1: Design Caption in Derendering Used in Stage 3 of the derendering pipeline to extract structured design intermediate representation (IR) from poster image, without any pre-computed bounding boxes. System prompt. You are senior visual designer and information architect specialised in academic posters. Return strict JSON description that downstream code can render back to HTML faithfully. User prompt. The MLLM receives single input: the original poster image. It is asked to identify high-level semantic regions entirely from visual observation (no layout annotations are provided) and, for each region, assign design tokens drawn from fixed vocabulary of 10 design dimensions (9 per-region + 1 global): global_decorations: solid_block_carrier / thin_divider_lines / logo_placeholder / qr_placeholder / background_pattern composition: grid_2col / grid_3col / flex_row / flex_col / absolute_overlap visual_anchor: scale_dominant / weight_dominant / contrast_dominant / isolated_focal flow: z_pattern / f_pattern / top_down / left_right interaction: solid_carrier / offset_underlay / partial_overlay / glass_morphism / flat_inline density: airy / balanced / dense color_scheme: neutral_palette / warm_palette / cool_palette typography: sans_modern / serif_classic / mono_technical emphasis: bold_caps / color_tint / icon_prefix / highlight_bg decoration: border_solid_square / border_dashed_square / border_solid_rounded / border_none_shadow / border_thick_accent Key rules. Region granularity: use 37 regions, one per major section (Header / Motivation / Method / Results / Conclusion). Sub-figures, columns, and sub-panels within the same section must not be split into separate regions. Dimension notes: for every dimension entry, concrete notes sentence is required describing the actual visual appearance (specific colours, paddings, weight hierarchy); restating the variant name verbatim is prohibited. Colour palette: the global palette must name four roles surface (background), primary (brand colour), accent (highlight), fg (foreground text)each as hex value observed in the image. Design caption: each region must include design_caption of 35 sentences describing its visual design holistically (colour usage, typographic hierarchy, density, decoration), without restating per-dimension variant names. RAP: Dataset for Paper-to-Poster Generation via Declarative Markup from Human-Crafted Exemplars PREPRINT Output. single JSON object with fields global_caption, global (palette, typography, decorations), and regions array. Each element of regions contains the region type, title, reading order, content caption, all 9 per-region dimension tokens (each {value, notes} pair), and free-form design_caption. No markdown fences, no commentary, no think blocks. B.2.2 Prompt 2: HTML Reconstruction in Derendering Used in Stage 4 of the derendering pipeline to convert the layout and design IR into pixel-faithful HTML/CSS reproduction of the poster. System prompt. You are an HTML/CSS reconstruction expert. Your goal: make the rendered HTML look identical to the attached reference image. User prompt. The MLLM receives five inputs: (1) the reference poster image (visual ground truth); (2) layout JSON containing, for every detected region, its bounding-box coordinates (xyxy, in pixels), semantic class label (title / plain text / figure / table / formula / . . . ), OCR-extracted text content, and OCR-measured font size (computed as crop_height/nlines 0.8); (3) the design specification produced by Prompt 1, comprising the global colour palette, typography family, page-level decoration types, and per-region design tokens (composition, visual_anchor, flow, interaction, density, color_scheme, typography, emphasis, decoration) each paired with free-form notes sentence; (4) dimensionCSS hints: for each enum variant the recommended CSS pattern (e.g. solid_carriera position:absolute background
at z-index:0 with coloured title strip; scaffold content divs raised to z-index:2); (5) font-size hints: per-block target font-size values; entries tagged [measured by OCR] are exact targets and must be reproduced precisely in CSS. Key rules. Geometry lock: every blocks left/top/width/height is immutable; the MLLM must not add, remove, or reorder scaffold
elements, and must not alter canvas dimensions. Text fidelity: for each text-like block, the MLLM must read the exact text from the reference imagereproducing every word, symbol, capitalisation, and line break. Mathematical expressions must be preserved using Unicode symbols, /, and CSS alignment; text must never overflow its bounding box. Style matching: the MLLM must match font family (sans-serif / serif / monospace), font size (using the OCRmeasured value as target), font weight and style, text colour, alignment, and line spacing as observed in the reference image. Region backgrounds: when regions interaction token is not flat_inline or its decoration token is not border_none_shadow, extra background
elements must be injected inside the canvas (z-index 0 for the outer coloured frame; z-index 1 for an inner white box if noted by the design caption) enclosing that regions blocks; scaffold block divs are then raised to z-index 2. Visual reproduction: all backgrounds, gradients, borders, divider lines, decorative shapes, header bars, and shadows must be reproduced using only CSS (background, border, box-shadow, border-radius, linear-gradient, ::before/::after); no external images or scripts are permitted. Design spec precedence: the design specification from Prompt 1 takes precedence over the MLLMs own interpretation of the reference image whenever they conflict. Output. Complete HTML from to . No markdown fences, no explanations, no

sections.title: C Evaluation Details
sections.content: C.1 Metrics C.1.1 Diversity Given the generated poster set { ˆPi}N metric pairwise over all (cid:0)N perceptually varied outputs across different input papers. 2 i=1 produced by method on the -sample test set, we compute each diversity (cid:1) pairs and report the average. Higher pairwise distances indicate more structurally and LPIPS [29]. Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity measures perceptual distance via weighted ℓ2 distance between deep feature activations of pretrained AlexNet. Higher mean pairwise LPIPS indicates that posters look more visually distinct to human perception across the generated set. DINOv2-CosDist. We extract global feature embedding from each poster using the pretrained DINOv2 [31] ViT-L/14 encoder and compute the cosine distance (1 cos) between every pair of embeddings. As DINOv2 is trained via self-supervision to capture high-level semantic and stylistic structure, larger DINOv2-CosDist values indicate that the generated posters span wider range of design styles and visual themes in the models semantic space, providing strong indicator of stylistic diversity beyond pixel-level variation. 20 RAP: Dataset for Paper-to-Poster Generation via Declarative Markup from Human-Crafted Exemplars PREPRINT DISTS [30]. Deep Image Structure and Texture Similarity extracts multi-scale VGG features and measures both structural and textural dissimilarity in distortion-tolerant manner. Higher mean pairwise DISTS indicates greater deep-feature diversity across the generated set. C.1.2 Human-Likeness To measure the distributional gap between generated posters and real human-created designs, we compute the Fréchet distance in different feature spaces. Given the feature representations of real posters (reference distribution r) and generated posters (generated distribution g), the Fréchet distance d2 is defined as: (cid:17) Σr + Σg 2(cid:112)ΣrΣg d2 = µr µg2 + Tr (4) (cid:16) where µ and Σ denote the mean vector and covariance matrix of the respective feature distributions. To capture different aspects of poster fidelity, we employ two metric variants by changing the underlying feature extractor: Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) [32]: Extracts 2048-dimensional features from the pool3 layer of an ImageNetpretrained InceptionV3 [33]. FID captures general image synthesis quality but is relatively insensitive to documentspecific layouts. Fréchet DINOv2 Distance (FDiD): Extracts 768-dimensional features from the pooler_output of self-supervised dinov2-base model [31]. By utilizing self-supervised vision transformer representations, FDiD is highly sensitive to visual structure, spatial arrangement, and layout geometry. Lower values across both metrics indicate that the generated posters are distributionally closer to real human designs.
